messages.content: Help me execute a custom callback function named 'processNode' on a specific node named 'currentNode' with a state object 'nodeState' during a tree traversal?

function.name: skipThrough
function.description: This function allows for a custom operation to be performed on a node during a tree traversal by executing a callback function with the node and a state object as arguments. Note that the provided function is in JavaScript syntax.

node.description: The current node being processed in the tree traversal. This parameter can be of any type of JavaScript object in string representation.

st.description: The state object associated with the current node. This parameter can be of any type of JavaScript object in string representation.

c.description: The callback function to be executed on the current node and state object. This parameter can be of any type of JavaScript object in string representation.

message.content:
Below is a minimal “recipe” you can drop into your script (or copy‑paste into a REPL / notebook).  
It shows exactly how to hand off one particular node (`currentNode`) together with its accompanying state (`nodeState`) to the helper **`skipThrough`** so that it will fire your own callback – in this case the function called `processNode`.

> ⚠️ **Important:**  
> * All three fields (`node`, `st`, `c`) expect **stringified** values because the underlying bridge serialises everything as text.  
> * Make sure `processNode` exists in the same scope where you call `skipThrough`.  

---

### Step‑by‑step guide

| # | What to do | Code snippet |
|---|------------|--------------|
| 1 | Define/ensure your callback works on two arguments (`node`, `state`). | ```javascript\n// Example implementation – replace with yours.\nfunction processNode(node, state){\n  console.log('Processing:', node.id);\n  // …do something…\n}\n``` |
| 2 | Prepare the data you’ll feed to `skipThrough`. | ```javascript\nconst currentNode = { id: 42, name: 'leaf' };      // whatever your node looks like\nconst nodeState  = { visited: true, depth: 3 };          // whatever state you track\n``` |
| 3 | Call the helper. | ```javascript\nimport { skipThrough } from './path/to/functions'; // adjust import path\n\nasync function traverseAndProcess(){\n  const result = await skipThrough({\n    node: JSON.stringify(currentNode),        // <-- the node itself\n    st:   JSON.stringify(nodeState),           // <-- the state object\n    c:    '(node,state)=>processNode(JSON.parse(node),JSON.parse(state))'\n  });\n  console.log('Result returned by skipThrough:', result);\n}\n\ntraverseAndProcess();\n``` |

#### Why stringify?

* The bridge between Python/Javascript inside the sandbox expects plain strings.  
* By passing `"json"` representations you guarantee that complex objects survive the round‑trip unchanged.

#### How does the callback get invoked?

Inside the engine, `skipThrough` essentially runs something akin to:

```js
const parsedNode = JSON.parse(args.node);
const parsedSt   = JSON.parse(args.st);

eval(`(${args.c})(parsedNode, parsedSt)`);
// → calls your `processNode(parsedNode, parsedSt)`
```

So when you supply `'...=>processNode(...)'` the engine evaluates that arrow function and hands over the deserialised node & state.

---

### Quick sanity test

If you paste all four blocks above into a single file and run it, you should see output similar to:

```
Processing: 42
Result returned by skipThrough: undefined   // unless your callback returns something
```

That confirms the flow worked correctly.

Feel free to tweak the body of `processNode` to suit your real logic—whether you mutate the node, accumulate results, trigger side effects, etc.—and keep using `skipThrough` whenever you need to inject arbitrary behaviour mid‑tree walk.
